name: llm-arena
desc: Free, open-source blind Elo arena for local LLMs on Windows — same prompts, hidden names, real win rates. 100 MB portable, offline, MIT.
features: ✅ **True blind mode** — model names hidden until you vote, so branding cannot bias the verdict
✅ **Elo ladder** — a running rating table built from your own votes with confidence intervals
✅ **Prompt sets** — load a folder of prompts and battle two models across all of them unattended
✅ **Speed telemetry** — tokens per second and time to first token recorded per response alongside quality votes
✅ **Bracket mode** — eliminate-style tournament across many models with a final standings board
✅ **Exportable results** — votes and ratings to CSV and JSON for blog posts or team decisions
✅ **100 MB self-contained exe** — runtime and inference backend bundled, portable, offline, MIT
compare: | Feature | **llm-arena** | LM Arena web | Open WebUI | SillyTavern |
| Price | **Free, MIT** | Free web | Free, OSS | Free, OSS |
| Local GGUF models in arena | **Yes** | No upload | No arena | No arena
| Blind A/B with vote | **Yes** | Yes | No | No |
| Speed telemetry per reply | **Yes** | No | Partial | Partial |
| Portable, no install | **Yes, 100 MB** | Browser | Docker | Node install
faqQ: which local LLM is actually better? how to compare models on your own PC
faqA: Leaderboards rank models on other people's hardware and prompts, which rarely matches your GPU and use case. llm-arena runs two of your GGUFs side by side in blind mode and builds an Elo table from your own votes. It is a 100 MB portable exe, MIT, fully offline — rankings never leave the machine.
s1: Dark arena (#121417, red #F87171): two response panels labeled A and B with names masked, vote buttons beneath, prompt card at top reading round 12.
s2: Elo ladder table: eight models ranked with rating, votes and confidence columns, sparkline per model, blue highlight on the current leader.
s3: Bracket mode: quarterfinal tree of eight model codenames, two nodes lit as active match, footer chip reading 28 of 50 prompts judged.
